interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — OPmobility (OPM.PA)

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used:** EUR 12.65 (live quote, 2026-08-31; previous close EUR 12.63; 52-week range EUR 12.30–18.16; market value about EUR 1.81 billion on 142.9 million shares outstanding)

**Transcripts reviewed:** two — the 2025 annual results call of 2026-02-25 and the first-half 2026 results call of 2026-07-22. Both were supplied with the middle of the call omitted, so the prepared remarks and the analyst question-and-answer session are complete but the detailed segment walk-through is not. Where a conclusion depends on material I could not see, I say so.

**Who this is.** OPmobility is the company formerly called Plastic Omnium. It makes plastic body parts for cars — bumpers and tailgates (the Exterior business), headlights and rear lights (Lighting), pre-assembled front-end modules that it ships straight to a carmaker's assembly line (Modules), and fuel tanks and battery or hydrogen storage systems (Powertrain, which the company calls C-Power and New Energies). Revenue was EUR 10.2 billion in 2025 on the consolidated accounts, or EUR 11.5 billion on what the company calls "economic revenue," a figure that adds in its share of jointly owned businesses in China and Korea. The Burelle family controls the company: only 37.2% of the shares trade freely, per the share-float data pulled today.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these two calls the story does not shift — it hardens defensively around the same three claims. That consistency is itself the most useful signal here.

**February 2026 (2025 results).** The new chief executive, Félicie Burelle, presenting for the first time after a family succession, framed 2025 as proof of a working strategy: "we took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." The pillars were geographic diversification (two-thirds of new orders won outside Europe), a strengthening balance sheet (net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation — a standard leverage gauge — falling from 1.7 times to 1.4 times), and a first crossing of the one-billion-euro mark in that earnings measure since 2019. The forward-looking additions were three: an announced transaction with Hyundai Mobis in lighting, a "beyond automotive" ambition anchored in battery packs and hydrogen for trucks and buses, and a robotaxi programme for an unnamed American electric-vehicle customer.

**July 2026 (first-half 2026 results).** The frame changed from proof to endurance. The single most important disclosure in either call is the market assumption reset: "we entered the 2026 year thinking that the market would be more or less flat, which, as you know, is not the case because today, the forecast for the 2026 year is minus 2.3%." That is a five-month-old plan already invalidated. The Chinese domestic market fell about 20% in the first half. Raw-material (resin) and energy costs bit, "mainly on Q2." The Middle East disruption, which had "very little impact" in the first quarter, had "more impact on Q2."

What was quietly demoted: the "beyond automotive" ambition, which in February had a stated but garbled revenue share and by July had shrunk to a passing mention. The robotaxi programme, introduced in February as a headline win, was described in July as having started "a bit lower than expected in terms of volume and in terms of complexity as well" — the first real walk-back in the file.

What was elevated: competitiveness and cost. In February the language was expansionary — order intake, launches, carbon neutrality. By July the emphasis is "there is no growth without being more competitive," robotics, digitalisation, and short-term costs "that we have postponed." That is a clean rotation from offence to defence in five months.

What did *not* change, and deserves credit: the deleveraging commitment, the fuel-tank market-share march, and the free-cash-flow guidance. Management reaffirmed in July that full-year free cash flow will exceed the EUR 297 million delivered in 2025, having banked EUR 165 million in the first half.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

### 2a. The most important finding: the screening metrics handed to this committee are wrong, and wrong in the direction of making the stock look cheaper than it is

OPmobility is a French company that reports twice a year, not four times. The data vendor files each half-year report as a "quarter." Any process that builds a trailing-twelve-month figure by summing four filed periods therefore sums **two years**, not one. That is exactly what happened here:

| Metric as supplied | What it actually is | Corrected figure |
|---|---|---|
| "TTM diluted EPS 2.49" | The sum of four half-years: EUR 0.71 (H1-26) + 0.67 (H2-25) + 0.63 (H1-25) + 0.49 (H2-24) = 2.50 — two full years of earnings | **EUR 1.37** trailing twelve months to 2026-06-30 (net income EUR 197m) |
| "TTM FCF 890M" | The same doubling: EUR 262m + 183m + 271m + 174m = 890m — two years of cash flow | **EUR 445m** on the vendor's definition; **about EUR 310m** on the company's own definition |
| "P/FCF 4.0x" | Understated by the same mechanism | **About 4.1x** on the vendor's cash-flow definition, **about 5.8x** on the company's |

The consequence is direct. On the supplied earnings figure the shares look like they trade at roughly 5 times earnings. On the true trailing figure they trade at **9.2 times**. On the analyst consensus for this year (EUR 1.54 per share, from nine covering houses) they trade at **8.2 times**; on 2027 (EUR 1.74) at **7.3 times**; on 2028 (EUR 1.92) at **6.6 times**.

That is still inexpensive. It is not the extraordinary bargain the input file implies, and the "deep value" classification this name arrived with rests substantially on a doubled denominator. Everything downstream must be re-struck on the corrected numbers.

A second supplied metric is not wrong so much as meaningless: **"beat 0/6 qtrs (0%)."** A company that does not report quarterly earnings and has no quarterly consensus cannot miss a quarterly consensus. This is an artefact of the same semi-annual filing pattern, not evidence of a chronic disappointment habit. Read as written it would defame a management team whose actual delivery record (section 4) is good.

### 2b. Management's claims against the real numbers

| Claim (and where) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "This is the first time since 2019 that the group is able to exceed EUR 1 billion in EBITDA" (Feb-26, CFO Olivier Dabi) | Vendor data shows EUR 840m for 2025 on the consolidated basis; the EUR 1.001bn is struck on "economic revenue" of EUR 11.5bn, which includes the company's share of joint ventures. Trailing twelve months to June 2026 is EUR 913m consolidated. | **True but basis-shifted.** The claim is defensible on the company's chosen measure; a reader comparing it to consolidated peers will overstate the business by roughly 10%. |
| "The debt was reduced in '25 by EUR 167 million and amounted to EUR 1.4 billion" (Feb-26) | Balance sheet at 2025-12-31: net debt EUR 1.515bn including EUR 320m of capitalised leases; EUR 1.195bn excluding them. At 2026-06-30: EUR 1.433bn including EUR 308m of leases, EUR 1.125bn excluding. | **Verified, on the lease-excluding definition** — which is the definition the company quotes. The reduction is real and continued into 2026 (about EUR 82m in the first half against the "EUR 90 million" claimed). This is the cleanest claim in the file. |
| "Free cash flow of EUR 297 million, up an impressive 20% versus '24" (Feb-26); "we did EUR 165 million in S1, and we confirm our guidance to exceed last year's" (Jul-26) | The company's own cash-flow definition is stricter than the vendor's, which shows EUR 445m for the trailing twelve months by charging a smaller capital-spending figure. Cash and equivalents rose from EUR 671m (Dec-24) to EUR 815m (Jun-26) while debt fell — the cash is arriving. | **Corroborated in direction, and the more conservative company number is the one to use.** |
| "Solid operating margin of 4.8% of our revenues" (Jul-26) | The vendor's mapping gives first-half 2026 operating income of EUR 219m on EUR 5,202m — 4.2% — against EUR 260m on EUR 5,332m a year earlier. On the company's economic-revenue basis, 4.8% is above the 4.3% struck for full-year 2025 (EUR 490m on EUR 11.5bn). | **Unresolved, and flagged.** The two sources point in opposite directions. Given the vendor's demonstrated aggregation failure on this filer (section 2a) and its unstable expense mapping (research and development recorded at EUR 139m in the first half of 2025 and zero in the first half of 2026), I weight the company's figure — but this is a claim I could not independently close, and the committee should treat the operating-margin trend as unverified rather than confirmed. |
| Market-share gains: "market share in C-Power has increased from 21% to 23% in 2025... on track with the target we have of 30% by 2030" (Feb-26, Stéphanie Laval) | Not independently verifiable from the financials supplied. What *is* corroborating: fuel tanks led first-half 2026 growth, helped by "slower electrification that benefited this activity." | **Plausible and internally consistent**, but it is management's own market definition and cannot be audited here. |
| "We managed again to show a slight growth in a decrease in market... like-for-like sales, we had a slight increase of our sales of 0.2%" (Jul-26) | Reported first-half revenue fell 2.4% (EUR 5,202m against EUR 5,332m). The gap is currency: the company flagged EUR 300m of adverse foreign-exchange in 2025 alone, mostly a weaker dollar. | **Verified as stated.** The like-for-like claim is honest; the reported line is worse, and the reported line is what pays the debt. |

### 2c. The quality of the cash flow deserves a second look

First-half 2026 operating cash flow of EUR 423 million included a **positive EUR 97 million swing in working capital, driven by a EUR 335 million increase in accounts payable** — that is, paying suppliers more slowly. Receivables went the other way, consuming EUR 155 million. Analyst Ross MacDonald put the question squarely: "Do I understand that the working capital benefits in the first half, close to EUR 100 million should fully reverse for the full year metrics?"

The chief financial officer did not say no. He said: "We're still going to have a push on WCR with supplier payments initiative that we started. We're going to have lower factoring, but we will definitely improve the gross cash flow. So all in all, we'll see a transfer between WCR and gross cash flow to meet our objectives."

Two things are conceded there. First, the working-capital contribution is expected to unwind. Second — and this was volunteered, not extracted — **factoring will be lower in the second half**. Factoring is selling receivables to a bank early to pull cash forward; less of it is a genuine cash headwind. So the second-half free-cash-flow bridge depends on operating profit improving enough to offset both a working-capital reversal and less receivable financing, in a market management has just told us is running 2.3% below where they planned. The guidance may well be met. But it is being met by a narrower path than the first-half print suggests.

### 2d. Returns are the number that matters, and they are poor

Return on invested capital of 6.0% and return on equity of 8.1% (as supplied, and consistent with net income of EUR 197 million on EUR 2.19 billion of equity). A European industrial with EUR 2.2 billion of debt-funded capital and a 35% tax rate almost certainly has a cost of capital above 6%. **This business, on current returns, does not create value by growing.** That is the central tension: the operating story is one of resilience and share gain, and the return profile is one of a capital-intensive supplier running to stand still.

The tax rate compounds it. Asked directly in February whether 35% holds, the finance chief answered: "Yes. Tax rate should remain stable at 35% in '26. We aim to improve it a little bit, but it should stay within this ballpark." A third of pre-tax profit leaves permanently.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Declining — but declining honestly, which is a different and better thing than declining evasively.**

*February 2026* — offensive and specific. "I'm focused and determined to keep on executing our strategy." "We took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." "Impressive performance." The chief financial officer opened with "very strong results, very solid results." Guidance was concrete and referenced against prior commitments.

*July 2026* — the adjectives survive ("a solid set of figures") but every one now arrives escorted by a qualifier: "despite, as you know, a very complex environment we are surrounded with." The defensive vocabulary is dense — "resilience," "mitigate," "monitor," "adapt," "postponed," "competitiveness." The chief executive twice describes herself as watching rather than acting: "we are carefully monitoring," "we again have to monitor what could be the impact for the second half."

The clearest single tell is the shift in how the future is discussed. In February the horizon was a plan. In July it is a scenario set: "we keep on running different scenarios." On price recovery in the second half: "it's really hard to anticipate, and it will all depend on... how the situation evolves." On the Chinese market: "we are not expecting big changes."

Crucially, specificity did **not** collapse. The market forecast was restated with a number (−2.3%), the first-half cash figure was given (EUR 165m), the full-year guidance was reaffirmed against a named prior-year bar (EUR 297m), the seasonality question was answered directly ("we expect the numbers to be broadly in line in H2 versus H1"). Managements that are about to disappoint usually go vaguer, not more precise. This one went more precise while going more defensive. That combination reads as a team absorbing a worse market rather than one concealing an internal problem.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High — with one unproven item outstanding.**

The one full guidance cycle visible in this file closed cleanly. In February 2026 the finance chief stated: "all in all, our '25 metrics was achieved — were achieved in line with the guidance that we gave last year and that we reiterated throughout the year." Every checkable component of that is corroborated by the balance sheet and cash-flow statements: debt down EUR 167 million, free cash flow up about 20% to EUR 297 million, leverage from 1.7 to 1.4 times.

Into 2026, three commitments have been made and one has already been tested:
- **Free cash flow above EUR 297 million** — reaffirmed 2026-07-22 with EUR 165 million banked. Half-delivered; the second half depends on the bridge described in section 2c. **This is the unproven item.**
- **Continued deleveraging** — delivered again in the first half (about EUR 82 million reduction).
- **Tax rate near 35%** — held.

No sandbagging pattern is visible; if anything the opposite. Management reaffirmed a rising cash-flow target into a market that had deteriorated 2.3 percentage points below their own planning assumption, which is the harder choice. They also declined to over-claim on the second half's margin, answering the seasonality question with "broadly in line" rather than promising expansion.

The "beat 0 of 6 quarters" figure in the supplied metrics should be disregarded entirely, for the reason given in section 2a.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Four topics recur, and management's handling ranges from candid to conspicuously thin.

**1. The Hyundai Mobis transaction — answered least, matters most.** Raised on both calls and never quantified. In February: "I appreciate you can't give the numbers on the balance sheet impact from the M&A you announced recently with Hyundai Mobis." In July, Michael Foundoukidis pressed on whether it fits inside the deleveraging target, and got: "All of the figures that we're disclosing are without anything linked to this project. But as we said, we are taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy."

Read that carefully. It is an *objective*, not a commitment, and the numbers presented to the market explicitly exclude the deal. The single largest capital-allocation decision in front of this company sits entirely outside the disclosed financial picture, five months after announcement. That is the biggest information gap in the file.

**2. The Varroc precedent, which management raised itself.** The last sizeable acquisition was the 2022 lighting purchase, and the chief executive's own description of it is damning: Lighting "continued to suffer from the poor order book of — prior to the acquisition." That is a self-reported diligence failure — they bought a business whose forward order book was worse than they had underwritten. MacDonald asked the obvious follow-up: is Mobis different? The answer was assertion, not evidence: "the situation is totally — it's not comparable... Now what we are considering here is a very sizable business with 1 leading OEM. More than 90% of its sales engaged with that."

That sentence is meant to reassure and does the opposite. **A target deriving more than 90% of sales from a single carmaker is not the cure for a bad order book; it is a different concentration risk of comparable severity.** Management is trading order-book uncertainty for customer-concentration certainty and presenting the trade as de-risking.

**3. Working capital and the honesty of the cash flow.** MacDonald pushed on this in both calls and got a straighter answer than on Mobis — see section 2c. Analysts are clearly modelling a second-half reversal; management has not disputed it.

**4. European restructuring, where management named its own tail risk.** Thomas Besson asked whether the current 80–90 basis points of annual restructuring effort would have to rise as European carmakers shift production out. The answer was unusually direct: "if those announcements were to be more and more frequent and obviously impacting us, then over the long run, yes, we would have to do more in terms of restructuring. But today, it's not embedded in our figures." **The last clause is the disclosure that matters.** A cost that management concedes is plausible is explicitly absent from the numbers the market is looking at.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody on either call asked what happens to the fuel-tank business — the most profitable part of the company and the one with the 30%-share ambition — when electrification eventually resumes. Management volunteered the reprieve ("slower electrification that benefited this activity") without anyone probing what happens when it ends. The terminal question sits unexamined on both calls.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **The plan was invalidated within five months.** Entered 2026 assuming a flat market; by July the forecast was −2.3%. Not management's fault; entirely management's problem.

🔴 **Returns below the cost of capital.** 6.0% return on invested capital, 8.1% on equity, a 35% tax rate. Growth here consumes value rather than creating it.

🔴 **The cash-flow bridge for the second half is narrower than the first-half print suggests** — a working-capital reversal plus explicitly lower factoring, against a weakening market (section 2c).

🔴 **A known future cost is deliberately outside the numbers.** European restructuring: "today, it's not embedded in our figures" (Jul-26).

🔴 **The largest capital decision is unquantified five months after announcement**, and the reassurance offered — a target with over 90% single-customer exposure — is itself a risk disclosure (section 5).

🔴 **No insider buying.** The supplied insider buy ratio is 0.00, with the shares 6% up from a 52-week low and roughly 30% below the 200-day average. In a family-controlled company where the family holds nearly two-thirds of the stock, the absence of any purchase at these levels is a signal by omission.

🔴 **The robotaxi programme underdelivered on its first outing** — "a bit lower than expected in terms of volume and in terms of complexity" (Jul-26) — the only concrete walk-back in the file, and it lands on the growth story management had led with in February.

🔴 **Gross margin compressed year on year** on the vendor data (9.6% in the first half of 2026 against 11.3%), consistent with management's own account of resin and energy costs biting in the second quarter, though the vendor's expense mapping on this filer is unreliable enough that I would not size a position on the precise figure.

🟢 **Deleveraging is real, repeated, and independently checkable** — the most credible thing in the file. Net debt down EUR 167 million in 2025 and about EUR 82 million more in the first half of 2026; leverage from 1.7 to 1.4 times; cash up from EUR 671 million to EUR 815 million while debt fell.

🟢 **Guidance has been delivered, and reaffirmed into a worse market** (section 4).

🟢 **The fuel-tank franchise is genuinely consolidating.** Share from 21% to 23%, in a market where, as management put it, "some players are decreasing, even disappearing."

🟢 **Outgrowing the market, modestly but consistently** — like-for-like growth of 0.2% against a market down 1% in the first half; growth in 2025 in a European market that shrank.

🟢 **The Lighting business is turning.** Three consecutive years of order intake, seven launches in the first half of 2026 with more to come, and a return to growth after 2025 was described plainly as "a low point in terms of sales."

🟢 **Geographic rebalancing is happening, not just announced** — two-thirds of 2025 order intake outside Europe; North America and the rest of Asia (Japan, Korea, India) led first-half 2026 growth.

🟢 **Management describes bad news in its own words before being asked.** "Unfortunately, 2025 was a low point"; the robotaxi shortfall; the restructuring tail. Candour of this kind is the cheapest available evidence of credibility, and it is present throughout.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**"Economic revenue" is doing quiet work.** The company's headline figures — EUR 11.5 billion of revenue, EUR 1.001 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation — are struck on a basis that includes its share of joint ventures it does not consolidate. The audited consolidated figures are EUR 10.2 billion and EUR 840 million. Neither presentation is improper, and the company is transparent about the basis. But it means the celebrated "first time above one billion since 2019" is a milestone on a measure that does not appear on the balance sheet, and the roughly EUR 454 million of equity-accounted investments sitting in non-current assets is where that value actually lives.

**"Local for local" has been repurposed.** In February it described a competitive advantage — 150 plants close to customers. By July it had become a shield: "we are pretty much local for local. So that's a big help when it comes to mitigating the impact of those events." The same fact, recast from offence to defence, is a small but telling barometer of the year.

**A new voice, structurally placed.** Stéphanie Laval now holds investor relations *and* strategic planning, which the chief executive framed deliberately: "you now have the same person helping me building the strategy and explaining needs to the market." That is a governance choice with two readings — better coherence between plan and disclosure, or a tighter grip on the narrative. Note that it is Laval, not the finance chief, who fields the market-share question — the most promotional number on the call is delivered by the person who owns both the plan and its communication.

**Deferred cost is disclosed but not sized.** "We also had to make some efforts in terms of monitoring some short-term costs that we have postponed, but nothing impacting, I would say, the overall strategy" (Jul-26). Postponed cost is borrowed margin. It is repaid.

**The hedge is narrower than it sounds.** "What we're hedging today is the energy. It's not the raw material topic." Resin — the actual input in a plastics business — is unhedged and managed through contractual pass-through clauses "and when it's not the case, discussing with our supplier and our customer." That is negotiation, not protection.

**Dependence on a policy that has no timetable.** Asked about the European Industrial Accelerator Act, the chief executive answered "Unfortunately, not" — no news, no time frame — and then described an industry lobbying for a framework where "the alignment is not full," closing with "otherwise it would be a bit too late." A meaningful part of the European recovery case rests on a regulatory outcome that management itself cannot date and does not control.

**Cash returned to shareholders is falling.** Dividends paid fell from EUR 54 million in the first half of 2025 to EUR 43 million in the first half of 2026 — roughly EUR 0.30 a share on the current count. Asked in February whether the dividend would be defended, the chief executive answered the principle rather than the number: "we always have a policy of serving dividend to the shareholders. So that should remain the case." The commitment is to paying *a* dividend, not *this* dividend.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

Not strengthening: returns sit below the cost of capital, gross margin is under pressure, the planning assumption for the year has already broken, and a real restructuring cost is acknowledged as absent from the numbers. Not deteriorating: debt is genuinely falling, cash is genuinely arriving, guidance has been met and reaffirmed into a worse market, the fuel-tank franchise is taking share in a consolidating market, and the Lighting business is recovering from a self-inflicted low. This is a competent, candid team holding a difficult position — neither compounding nor cracking.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.**

Not the market, and not the Mobis deal. It is this: **once the doubled-period error in the supplied metrics is corrected, the discount largely disappears.** The shares trade at 9.2 times trailing earnings and 8.2 times this year's consensus, on an enterprise value (market value plus net debt) of about EUR 3.24 billion against roughly EUR 913 million of trailing operating cash earnings — about 3.6 times. Its two closest French peers, Valeo and Forvia, trade at about 2.4 and 2.7 times the same measure today. **OPmobility is not trading at a discount to its direct comparables; it trades at a premium of roughly 35–45%** — a premium I judge deserved, since it is the only one of the three earning a consistent profit and cutting debt, but a premium nonetheless. The name arrived here labelled a deep bargain. It is a fairly-priced-to-modestly-cheap, competently-run, low-return cyclical.

And because roughly 44% of that enterprise value is debt, a 10% shortfall in operating earnings moves the equity roughly 18%. There is no floor underneath: tangible book value, after stripping EUR 1.30 billion of goodwill and EUR 0.79 billion of other intangibles from EUR 2.19 billion of equity, is about EUR 0.70 a share. Position size should reflect a levered cyclical with no asset backstop, not a cheap compounder.

**Economic moat.**

*Type:* scale-cost, concentrated in one place. The fuel-tank business (C-Power) has the real thing — roughly 23% of a global market that is consolidating as competitors exit, with programme-life switching costs that make a carmaker's decision effectively irreversible for the life of a vehicle. Exterior is scale-cost but commoditising. Modules is contract assembly with no moat at all — it is high-revenue, low-margin work that exists because the company is already on site. Lighting is sub-scale and was bought impaired.

*Width:* **NARROW.** The evidence is unambiguous on this point: a 6.0% return on invested capital is not what a wide moat looks like. Wide moats produce returns comfortably above the cost of capital across a cycle; this one does not clear it at all. The moat is real but confined to perhaps a fifth of revenue, and the rest of the business dilutes it back to a market return.

*Trend:* **STABLE.** Share is rising (21% to 23%, targeting 30%), operating earnings crossed one billion euros for the first time since 2019, and the balance sheet is strengthening — all widening forces. Against that, gross margin is compressing and unhedged resin costs are being negotiated rather than passed through automatically. The two roughly offset. This is not a franchise being eroded, and it is not one being built.

*Secular threat:* **MATERIAL, not terminal** — and the theme is the energy transition. The fuel-tank business is the most profitable part of the company and its base disappears with the internal combustion engine. Right now that is a tailwind: management explicitly credited "slower electrification that benefited this activity" for first-half 2026 growth. **That is a cyclical reprieve inside a secular decline, and it should not be mistaken for durability.** The reason the threat is material rather than terminal is that roughly four-fifths of the business — bumpers, tailgates, lights, front-end modules — is indifferent to what powers the car, and the company is deliberately building battery-pack and hydrogen storage capability on the same manufacturing base. Autonomous driving, the other structural force in this industry, is a modest tailwind here rather than a threat: OPmobility supplies parts for a robotaxi programme today.

*Fear-print or value trap?* **Neither, cleanly — and that is the honest answer.** It is not a value trap: the earnings base is not structurally shrinking, debt is falling, and the company is winning share. But it is not a mispricing either, because after correcting the data error the price sits close to fair, at a premium to its nearest peers rather than a discount. The cheapness that brought this name to the committee was substantially arithmetic, not opportunity.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
OPmobility is a competent, family-controlled French car-parts maker whose shares, at EUR 12.65 on the Paris market (live quote, 31 August 2026), sit within about 3% of a 52-week low of EUR 12.30 after falling roughly 30% from EUR 18.16 a year ago. The bullish case does not need the European car market to boom. It needs three things that are already happening to keep happening.

First, the balance sheet is genuinely repairing, and this is the most checkable claim in the file. Net debt fell EUR 167 million in 2025 to about EUR 1.4 billion and fell roughly EUR 82 million more in the first half of 2026, while cash on hand rose from EUR 671 million at the end of 2024 to EUR 815 million at 30 June 2026. Leverage came down from 1.7 times to 1.4 times operating cash earnings (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation). Free cash flow was EUR 297 million in 2025, up about 20%, and management reaffirmed on 22 July 2026 that 2026 will exceed that, having banked EUR 165 million in the first half. In a market that now rewards businesses whose own cash covers their spending rather than businesses promising future returns, this profile is on the right side of the line.

Second, the fuel-tank business is a real franchise that is consolidating. Management reported global share rising from 21% to 23%, targeting 30% by 2030, in a market where, as they put it in February 2026, 'some players are decreasing, even disappearing.' Switching costs here are severe: once a tank is designed into a vehicle programme, it stays for the life of that programme. And the near-term environment helps rather than hurts. On the July 2026 call, first-half growth was credited to fuel tanks helped by 'slower electrification that benefited this activity.' The very force the market fears is arriving later than feared.

Third, the company keeps outgrowing a shrinking market. Like-for-like sales rose 0.2% in the first half of 2026 against a market down about 1%, driven by North America and by Asia outside China. Two-thirds of 2025 order intake was won outside Europe. The Lighting business, bought impaired in 2022 and described by the chief executive as having hit 'a low point in terms of sales' in 2025, has now had three consecutive years of order intake and returned to growth with seven launches in the first half and more scheduled.

Put those together and the earnings path the market is underwriting is modest and plausibly beatable. Nine covering analysts have consensus earnings per share of EUR 1.54 for 2026, EUR 1.74 for 2027 and EUR 1.92 for 2028, with operating cash earnings recovering from about EUR 886 million to about EUR 967 million. At EUR 12.65 the shares change hands at 8.2 times this year's consensus and 6.6 times 2028's. If European light-vehicle production simply stops getting worse, if the promised free cash flow lands, and if the Hyundai Mobis lighting transaction is completed without breaking the deleveraging path, a sum-of-the-parts valuation (valuing each business line separately) supports roughly EUR 19 a share.

Conditions the bull case depends on, stated plainly: full-year 2026 free cash flow above EUR 297 million without a collapse in the second half; net debt continuing to fall through the Mobis transaction; the fuel-tank share march staying on its stated path; and European restructuring costs not stepping materially above the current 80 to 90 basis points a year. Management named that last risk itself and confirmed it is 'not embedded in our figures.'
bear_thesis:
The bearish case starts with an uncomfortable finding about the numbers this name arrived with, and then compounds it with a cyclical and a structural problem.

The screening data overstated how cheap this is, by roughly a factor of two. OPmobility reports twice a year, not four times, and the data feed files each half-year report as a quarter. A trailing-twelve-month figure built by summing four filed periods therefore sums two years. The supplied trailing earnings per share of EUR 2.49 is exactly the sum of four half-years (EUR 0.71 plus 0.67 plus 0.63 plus 0.49); true trailing earnings per share to 30 June 2026 are EUR 1.37. The supplied trailing free cash flow of EUR 890 million is the same doubling of EUR 445 million. Corrected, the shares trade at 9.2 times trailing earnings, not about 5 times. On enterprise value (market value plus net debt) of about EUR 3.24 billion against trailing operating cash earnings of about EUR 913 million, the multiple is about 3.6 times, against Valeo at roughly 2.4 times and Forvia at roughly 2.7 times on the same measure today. The stock is not at a discount to its nearest peers; it is at a premium.

Second, the returns do not justify the capital. Return on invested capital is 6.0% and return on equity 8.1%, against a tax rate management confirmed will stay near 35% ('should remain stable at 35% in 26'). For a capital-intensive supplier carrying EUR 2.25 billion of gross debt, a 6% return is at or below the cost of that capital. This business does not create value by growing. Every euro of the roughly EUR 500 million annual capital programme is, on current returns, a euro that earns about what it costs.

Third, the cycle is still deteriorating and the plan has already broken once. Management entered 2026 assuming a 'more or less flat' market; by 22 July the forecast was minus 2.3%. The Chinese domestic market fell about 20% in the first half. Resin and energy costs bit 'mainly on Q2,' and resin is explicitly unhedged: 'what we are hedging today is the energy. It is not the raw material topic.' Recovery of those costs from customers is negotiated case by case, and on the ability to recover in the second half the chief executive said it is 'really hard to anticipate.'

Fourth, the second-half cash-flow bridge is narrower than the first-half print suggests. First-half operating cash flow of EUR 423 million included a positive EUR 97 million working-capital swing driven by a EUR 335 million rise in payables, that is, paying suppliers more slowly. Asked directly whether that reverses, the finance chief did not deny it and volunteered a second headwind: 'we are going to have lower factoring' - less selling of receivables early to pull cash forward. So the full-year cash guidance now needs operating profit to improve enough to absorb both a working-capital reversal and reduced receivable financing, in a market running 2.3 points below plan.

Fifth, a real cost is deliberately outside the numbers. Asked whether European restructuring would have to step up as carmakers move production out, the chief executive answered 'over the long run, yes, we would have to do more in terms of restructuring. But today, it is not embedded in our figures.'

Sixth, the largest capital decision is unquantified. The Hyundai Mobis lighting transaction was announced by February 2026 and, as of the 22 July 2026 call, still had no disclosed balance-sheet impact: 'all of the figures that we are disclosing are without anything linked to this project,' with only an 'objective' - not a commitment - that it will not disturb deleveraging. The precedent is poor: the 2022 lighting acquisition 'continued to suffer from the poor order book of prior to the acquisition,' a self-reported diligence failure. And the reassurance offered about the new target is itself a risk disclosure - 'more than 90% of its sales engaged with' one carmaker.

Finally, there is no floor. Strip EUR 1.30 billion of goodwill and EUR 0.79 billion of other intangibles from EUR 2.19 billion of equity and tangible book value is about EUR 0.70 a share. About 44% of enterprise value is debt, so a 10% shortfall in operating cash earnings moves the equity roughly 18%. No insider has bought: the supplied insider buy ratio is 0.00, in a company where the controlling family holds nearly two-thirds of the stock and the shares are near a 52-week low.

What would confirm the bear case: full-year 2026 free cash flow landing at or below EUR 297 million; the Mobis transaction disclosed with a debt-funded price that lifts leverage back above 1.6 times; a restructuring charge appearing in the 2026 accounts; or European light-vehicle production forecasts cut again into 2027.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the screen suggested, and it points the opposite way from the one that brought this name here.

The screen's premise was that the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable earnings power. Half of that is right and half is an arithmetic error. The error first: because OPmobility reports twice a year and the data feed files each half-year as a quarter, the supplied trailing earnings per share of EUR 2.49 is two years of earnings summed, and the supplied trailing free cash flow of EUR 890 million is two years of cash summed. The true figures are EUR 1.37 and about EUR 445 million. So the apparent 5-times earnings multiple is really 9.2 times, and the apparent bargain is a fair price. Any disagreement with the market has to survive that correction, and most of it does not.

What does survive is a genuine and specific disagreement, and it concerns the fuel-tank business. Nine analysts model 2026 earnings of EUR 1.54, 2027 of EUR 1.74 and 2028 of EUR 1.92 - a steady climb of about 12% a year that implicitly assumes the cyclical trough is behind and nothing structural interferes. Neither half of that is safe. On the near side, management told the market on 22 July 2026 that their own year-opening assumption of a 'more or less flat' market had already been replaced by a forecast of minus 2.3%, that the Chinese domestic market fell about 20% in the first half, and that recovering resin and energy costs from customers in the second half is 'really hard to anticipate.' The 2026 consensus was struck before or around that reset and looks stale at the top end. On the far side, the street's 2028 number implicitly capitalises a fuel-tank profit stream whose base disappears with the internal combustion engine. Management themselves credited first-half growth to 'slower electrification that benefited this activity.' A delay is being read as durability.

There is a second, cleaner disagreement, and it is with our own peer file rather than with the street. That file called the valuation in line with Valeo and Forvia. Re-struck live today, OPmobility trades at about 3.6 times enterprise value to trailing operating cash earnings against Valeo at 2.4 and Forvia at 2.7 - a 35% to 45% premium, not parity. The premium is deserved, because OPmobility is the only one of the three earning a consistent profit while cutting debt. But a deserved premium is not an edge. Correctly seen, the market is already paying up for exactly the quality this committee would want to buy.

The one place the street may be genuinely too gloomy is the balance sheet. Deleveraging here has been delivered twice in a row and is independently verifiable - net debt down EUR 167 million in 2025 and about EUR 82 million more in the first half of 2026, cash up from EUR 671 million to EUR 815 million while debt fell. In a tape that has just spent two months re-pricing companies on whether their own cash covers their spending, that profile is worth more than the multiple implies. That is a real but modest disagreement, and it is worth perhaps a point of multiple, not a re-rating.
forcing_function:
There is no hard date that forces a re-rating, and the committee should not pretend otherwise. What exists is one dated settlement of a promise, one undated corporate event and one undated political outcome.

The dated one is full-year 2026 results, due around late February 2027 based on the 25 February 2026 timing of the prior year's presentation. That is when management's reaffirmed commitment to exceed EUR 297 million of free cash flow is settled, and when we learn whether the second-half working-capital reversal and reduced factoring were absorbed. It is also when a European restructuring charge, if one is taken, would surface. The date is fixed; the outcome is not contracted, and company guidance carries no obligation. This is the event most likely to move the shares in either direction, and it is roughly six months away.

The undated corporate event is completion and disclosure of the Hyundai Mobis lighting transaction. When the price, financing and order book are finally published, the market gets its first hard read on whether this management can buy well after the 2022 lighting purchase went wrong, and whether the deleveraging path survives. A transaction completed at a modest price and funded from cash flow would validate the balance-sheet story and is the single most plausible route to a re-rating; a debt-funded price would do the reverse. No closing date has been given in either call.

The undated political outcome is the European Industrial Accelerator Act, the local-content framework the whole European supplier group is lobbying for. Asked for a time frame on 22 July 2026, the chief executive said 'Unfortunately, not,' and described an industry where 'the alignment is not full.' A concrete framework would re-rate the entire sector at once. That is precisely why it should be discounted heavily as a reason to own this particular name: it is a shared driver that would lift Valeo and Forvia identically, and this month's regime work is explicit about being wary of theses hinging on one shared macro factor.

Two things that are often mistaken for forcing functions and are not, here. There is no activist path - the controlling family sees to that. And there is no buyback authorisation or asset-sale process in evidence in either call. The re-rating, if it comes, comes from cash flow arriving on schedule and debt continuing to fall, half-year after half-year, until the market pays a normal multiple for it. That is a slow forcing function, and it is the only honest one on offer.
valley_of_death:
The risky window runs from now through the full-year results in late February 2027, and there are four distinct hazards in it.

First and most likely: the second-half cash-flow bridge. First-half operating cash flow of EUR 423 million was flattered by a positive EUR 97 million working-capital swing, driven by a EUR 335 million rise in amounts owed to suppliers - that is, paying them more slowly. An analyst asked on 22 July whether that fully reverses; the finance chief did not deny it, and volunteered a second headwind: 'we are going to have lower factoring,' meaning less selling of receivables early to pull cash forward. So delivering full-year free cash flow above EUR 297 million now requires operating profit to improve enough to absorb both a working-capital reversal and reduced receivable financing, in a market management has told us is running 2.3 percentage points below their own planning assumption. This is the most probable disappointment in the file, and it lands squarely on the one metric the equity story rests on.

Second: an acquisition priced in the dark. The Hyundai Mobis lighting transaction has been announced since at least February 2026 and, as of 22 July, still carried no disclosed price, financing or closing date, and sat entirely outside the reported figures. Management offered an objective that it will not disturb deleveraging, not a commitment. If it completes debt-funded at a size that lifts leverage back toward or above 1.6 times operating cash earnings, the single most credible plank of the bull case is removed in one announcement. The precedent is not reassuring: the 2022 lighting purchase 'continued to suffer from the poor order book of prior to the acquisition,' and the new target reportedly draws 'more than 90% of its sales' from one carmaker.

Third: a restructuring charge that everyone knows is coming and nobody has booked. Asked whether European restructuring must step up as carmakers move production out, the chief executive said 'over the long run, yes, we would have to do more,' then added the sentence that matters: 'today, it is not embedded in our figures.' European restructuring is expensive by management's own account. A charge appearing in the 2026 accounts would hit reported earnings and cash simultaneously.

Fourth: input costs with no hedge. Resin, the actual raw material of a plastics business, is explicitly unhedged - 'what we are hedging today is the energy. It is not the raw material topic' - and is managed through contract clauses and, failing those, negotiation. Management noted resin prices had relieved for a few weeks and were 'moving up again,' with Middle East disruption having escalated from 'very little impact' in the first quarter to 'more impact on Q2.'

There is no debt maturity wall to add to this: gross debt of EUR 2.25 billion sits against EUR 815 million of cash with only EUR 662 million falling due within a year, and leverage at 1.4 times is comfortable. The danger here is earnings and gearing, not refinancing. But because roughly 44% of enterprise value is debt, the equity moves about 1.8 times any earnings shortfall - so a 10% miss on operating cash earnings is an 18% move in the shares, from a price that already offers only about 22% upside to our central fair value.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical liquidation event here, and that is precisely the problem - this is a slow bleed, not a flush, which is why waiting for a capitulation low may mean waiting a long time.

The ownership structure explains most of it. Only 37.2% of the shares trade freely: 53.2 million of 142.9 million shares, worth about EUR 670 million at EUR 12.65. The Burelle family controls the balance. That has three consequences. It puts a floor under how far forced selling can go, because roughly two-thirds of the register cannot be forced out. It also caps how fast any recovery can be bought, because the tradeable stock is thin - about EUR 500,000 changed hands in the session observed today. And it closes off the activist path entirely: there is no proxy campaign, no board seat and no strategic review that an outside investor can force on a family holding a controlling stake. The classic special-situation lever is simply unavailable on this name.

The income-focused holder is being tested, quietly. Cash dividends paid fell from EUR 54 million in the first half of 2025 to EUR 43 million in the first half of 2026, roughly EUR 0.30 a share on the current count - a yield of about 2.4%, thin for a European industrial and thin enough that a dividend-mandated fund has little reason to stay. Asked in February whether the payout would be defended, the chief executive answered the principle and not the number: 'we always have a policy of serving dividend to the shareholders. So that should remain the case.' That is a commitment to paying a dividend, not to paying this one. A further trim would remove the last mechanical reason for income funds to hold, but the amounts involved are too small to produce a violent exit - the register would simply keep thinning.

Index and scale pressure works the same slow way. At a market value of about EUR 1.81 billion and a free float near EUR 670 million, this is a small company by European standards and getting smaller as the price falls. Continued drift risks demotion out of mid-cap benchmarks, which brings passive selling - but that selling arrives as a scheduled, well-telegraphed rebalance, not a shock, and this month's regime work is explicit that the mechanical index print no longer reliably pays.

The most informative positioning fact is an absence. The supplied insider buy ratio is 0.00. The shares sit about 3% above a 52-week low of EUR 12.30, roughly 30% below the EUR 18.16 they fetched a year ago and about 16% below the 200-day average. A controlling family that believes its own recovery narrative and knows the undisclosed acquisition terms has not bought a share. That is not proof of anything, but it is the cheapest signal available and it is silent.
moderator_conclusion:
My call is to wait, and to be specific about what I am waiting for.

This name arrived flagged as a deep bargain, and the single most important thing this committee needs to know is that the bargain was largely an arithmetic error. OPmobility reports twice a year, and the data feed files each half-year report as a quarter, so a trailing-twelve-month figure assembled from four filed periods sums two years. The supplied trailing earnings per share of EUR 2.49 is exactly EUR 0.71 plus EUR 0.67 plus EUR 0.63 plus EUR 0.49; the true figure is EUR 1.37. The supplied trailing free cash flow of EUR 890 million is the same doubling of EUR 445 million. Corrected, the shares at EUR 12.65 trade at 9.2 times trailing earnings and 8.2 times this year's consensus - respectable, not remarkable. And measured on enterprise value against operating cash earnings, about 3.6 times, OPmobility trades at a 35% to 45% premium to Valeo and Forvia, its two nearest French peers, not at a discount to them.

That premium is deserved, which is the second thing worth saying. This is a well-run business with a candid management team. Debt has fallen two years running and the reduction is independently verifiable on the balance sheet - cash up from EUR 671 million to EUR 815 million while borrowings came down. Free cash flow guidance has been met and then reaffirmed into a market that deteriorated below management's own planning assumption, which is the harder choice. The fuel-tank business is a real franchise taking share where competitors are exiting. Management describes its own bad news before being asked - the robotaxi programme starting 'a bit lower than expected,' Lighting hitting 'a low point,' European restructuring that 'today is not embedded in our figures.' Candour of that kind is the cheapest evidence of credibility there is, and it is present throughout. Our deep dive on management scored the team 4 out of 5 with a stable trajectory.

So why not buy it. Three reasons, in order of weight.

The arithmetic of the opportunity is simply not compelling. Our central sum-of-the-parts fair value is EUR 15.40 a share - about 22% above today's price - and reaching it already requires accepting that this company deserves a 40% valuation premium to its peer group. The adverse case is EUR 7.80. We would be risking roughly EUR 4.85 to make roughly EUR 2.75. There is no floor beneath that: no deal terms, no net cash, and tangible book value of about EUR 0.70 a share once goodwill and other intangibles come out. With roughly 44% of enterprise value in debt, the equity moves about 1.8 times any earnings shortfall.

The returns do not support a long hold at this price. Return on invested capital is 6.0% against a tax rate management has confirmed stays near 35%. This business does not create value by growing; it runs to stand still. A low multiple on a low-return, capital-hungry business is not the same opportunity as a low multiple on a compounder, and that difference is exactly what separates a fair price from a bargain.

And the cycle is still going the wrong way. Management entered 2026 planning for a flat market and by July was working with a forecast of minus 2.3%. The second-half cash-flow bridge is narrower than the first-half headline implies - a working-capital reversal plus explicitly lower receivable financing - and the largest capital decision in front of the company, the Hyundai Mobis lighting acquisition, still has no disclosed price five months after announcement, with a target that reportedly draws more than 90% of its sales from a single carmaker.

On the market backdrop: this month's regime read favours businesses whose own cash covers their spending over businesses promising future returns, and on that test OPmobility scores well - it is a cash-generative deleverager, not a story, and nothing in this thesis depends on rate cuts. But the same read warns against theses that hinge on one shared macro factor, and the recovery case here rests almost entirely on European light-vehicle production plus a policy framework management cannot date. That is precisely the shared-driver dependence to be wary of, and it would lift Valeo and Forvia identically, so none of it is edge specific to this name. The catalysts themselves are soft and have no fixed date, which under this book's rules is neither a mark for nor against - the event-driven names live elsewhere, and what I am judging here is the residual value case on its own.

What I am waiting for, precisely. Either a price near or below EUR 10.50, which would open a discount of roughly a third to our central fair value and turn the risk and reward the right way up; or, at a higher price, one of two developments: full-year 2026 results in late February 2027 confirming free cash flow above EUR 297 million without a second-half working-capital collapse, or the Hyundai Mobis transaction disclosed at a price funded from cash flow that leaves leverage at or below 1.4 times. Either would convert this from a fairly-priced cyclical into something I would underwrite.

On the value case judged entirely on its own, ignoring every catalyst and every market condition, I score it 2 out of 5. The franchise is real and the accounts are clean, but a 22% gap to a generously-struck fair value, on a business earning 6% on its capital, is not a margin of safety. The moat is narrow and confined to the fuel-tank business, currently stable rather than widening, and the structural threat from electrification is material - it takes the most profitable fifth of the company - though not terminal, because bumpers, tailgates, lights and modules do not care what powers the car. The current benefit from slower electrification is a delay, not durability. It should not be capitalised as one.
sop_fair_value: EUR 15.40 per share (range EUR 14.50 to EUR 16.50)
sop_breakdown:
Base case, reconciling the favourable and adverse cases, struck on consensus 2026 operating cash earnings of about EUR 886 million on consolidated revenue of about EUR 10.1 billion, with multiples set between the two cases:
- Powertrain, mostly fuel tanks (about EUR 300 million of operating cash earnings at 5.0 times): EUR 1.50 billion, the largest single contributor. It earns the highest multiple in the group for 23% global share rising toward a stated 30% by 2030 and programme-life switching costs; capped below the favourable multiple because the base itself is powertrain-dependent.
- Exterior and Lighting (about EUR 400 million at 3.2 times): EUR 1.28 billion. The historic franchise, with Lighting recovering from a 2025 low.
- Modules (about EUR 186 million at 2.9 times): EUR 0.54 billion. Contract assembly, no moat, but real cash.
- Equity-accounted joint ventures at three-quarters of carrying value: EUR 0.34 billion. These sit outside consolidated earnings and account for the gap between the company's EUR 11.5 billion economic revenue and its EUR 10.2 billion consolidated revenue.
Gross value EUR 3.66 billion; less net debt of EUR 1.433 billion at 30 June 2026 (lease-inclusive, matching the lease-inclusive earnings measure) and EUR 32 million of minority interests; equity value EUR 2.20 billion on 142.9 million shares = EUR 15.40.

The implied blended multiple is 3.75 times operating cash earnings. That is about a 40% premium to Valeo (2.4 times) and Forvia (2.7 times) today, and it is the assumption the whole valuation rests on. I judge the premium deserved - OPmobility is the only one of the three earning a consistent profit and cutting debt - but a reader should understand that if the peer group is right and OPmobility deserves no premium, fair value falls to roughly EUR 11. Cross-checks: 2027 consensus earnings of EUR 1.74 at 8.5 times gives EUR 14.80; sustainable free cash flow of about EUR 310 million capitalised at a 12% yield, appropriate for a levered cyclical, gives about EUR 17.50. No structural floor exists - no deal terms, no net cash, and tangible book value of about EUR 0.70 a share.
risk_reward: Unfavourable at EUR 12.65. Downside to the adverse case of EUR 7.80 is about EUR 4.85 a share; upside to the EUR 15.40 base-case fair value is about EUR 2.75 a share. In other words the committee is being asked to risk close to twice what it stands to make on the central case, and the base case itself already assumes a 40% valuation premium to the two nearest peers. Reaching the favourable EUR 19.25 requires both a European production recovery and successful completion of an acquisition whose price is still undisclosed. There is no structural floor to lean on: tangible book value is about EUR 0.70 a share and roughly 44% of enterprise value is debt, so the equity moves about 1.8 times any change in operating earnings. The reward improves materially below about EUR 10.50, where the discount to base-case fair value reaches roughly a third.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note:
The peer file supplies Valeo, Forvia, Continental, 'MG' and Aptiv, with a verdict of in line. I re-struck every multiple live today rather than relying on the file's or my own recollection, and the conclusion changes materially.

First, a data correction. The ticker 'MG' in the peer list does not resolve to Magna International, which trades as MGA. It resolves to a company with a market value of about USD 0.6 billion and roughly USD 0.74 billion of revenue - not a car-parts peer at all. I have excluded it rather than let it anchor anything.

Second, the live anchors. On enterprise value (market value plus net debt) divided by trailing operating cash earnings, the current readings are: Valeo about 2.4 times, Forvia about 2.7 times, Aptiv about 7.9 times and Continental about 10.5 times. The last two are not usable comparables today - both have recently separated businesses, both show distorted trailing figures including negative returns on equity, and both are electronics-led rather than plastics-led. The honest anchor is Valeo and Forvia at 2.4 to 2.7 times.

OPmobility, at EUR 12.65 with net debt of EUR 1.433 billion, carries an enterprise value of about EUR 3.24 billion against about EUR 913 million of trailing operating cash earnings - roughly 3.6 times. That is a 35% to 45% premium to its two nearest French peers, not a discount. The peer file's 'in line' verdict was reached on a price-to-free-cash-flow figure that inherited the doubled-period error described in the deep dive; corrected, the relative-value lever runs against this name on earnings-based multiples. On revenue-based multiples the ranking flips - OPmobility trades at about 0.32 times enterprise value to sales against Valeo at 0.36 and Forvia at 0.41 - but that reflects its structurally lower margin, not a bargain.

Third, and most important for how much credit to take: this entire group is being repriced on the same unresolved drivers - the pace of electrification, Chinese competition, European production volumes and tariffs. The gap between OPmobility and its peers is therefore shared-factor sector beta, not name-specific edge, and none of it should be booked as alpha unique to this company. The one genuine idiosyncratic difference is quality, and it favours OPmobility: it is the only one of the three generating consistent net income (return on equity 8.1%, against Valeo's 6.0% and a deeply negative figure at Forvia) while reducing net debt. That is what justifies the premium it already trades at - and it means the premium is the fair state of affairs, not an opportunity.

# Forensic Dossier — OPmobility (OPM.PA)

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used:** EUR 12.65 (live quote, 2026-08-31; previous close EUR 12.63; 52-week range EUR 12.30–18.16; market value about EUR 1.81 billion on 142.9 million shares outstanding)

**Transcripts reviewed:** two — the 2025 annual results call of 2026-02-25 and the first-half 2026 results call of 2026-07-22. Both were supplied with the middle of the call omitted, so the prepared remarks and the analyst question-and-answer session are complete but the detailed segment walk-through is not. Where a conclusion depends on material I could not see, I say so.

**Who this is.** OPmobility is the company formerly called Plastic Omnium. It makes plastic body parts for cars — bumpers and tailgates (the Exterior business), headlights and rear lights (Lighting), pre-assembled front-end modules that it ships straight to a carmaker's assembly line (Modules), and fuel tanks and battery or hydrogen storage systems (Powertrain, which the company calls C-Power and New Energies). Revenue was EUR 10.2 billion in 2025 on the consolidated accounts, or EUR 11.5 billion on what the company calls "economic revenue," a figure that adds in its share of jointly owned businesses in China and Korea. The Burelle family controls the company: only 37.2% of the shares trade freely, per the share-float data pulled today.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these two calls the story does not shift — it hardens defensively around the same three claims. That consistency is itself the most useful signal here.

**February 2026 (2025 results).** The new chief executive, Félicie Burelle, presenting for the first time after a family succession, framed 2025 as proof of a working strategy: "we took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." The pillars were geographic diversification (two-thirds of new orders won outside Europe), a strengthening balance sheet (net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation — a standard leverage gauge — falling from 1.7 times to 1.4 times), and a first crossing of the one-billion-euro mark in that earnings measure since 2019. The forward-looking additions were three: an announced transaction with Hyundai Mobis in lighting, a "beyond automotive" ambition anchored in battery packs and hydrogen for trucks and buses, and a robotaxi programme for an unnamed American electric-vehicle customer.

**July 2026 (first-half 2026 results).** The frame changed from proof to endurance. The single most important disclosure in either call is the market assumption reset: "we entered the 2026 year thinking that the market would be more or less flat, which, as you know, is not the case because today, the forecast for the 2026 year is minus 2.3%." That is a five-month-old plan already invalidated. The Chinese domestic market fell about 20% in the first half. Raw-material (resin) and energy costs bit, "mainly on Q2." The Middle East disruption, which had "very little impact" in the first quarter, had "more impact on Q2."

What was quietly demoted: the "beyond automotive" ambition, which in February had a stated but garbled revenue share and by July had shrunk to a passing mention. The robotaxi programme, introduced in February as a headline win, was described in July as having started "a bit lower than expected in terms of volume and in terms of complexity as well" — the first real walk-back in the file.

What was elevated: competitiveness and cost. In February the language was expansionary — order intake, launches, carbon neutrality. By July the emphasis is "there is no growth without being more competitive," robotics, digitalisation, and short-term costs "that we have postponed." That is a clean rotation from offence to defence in five months.

What did *not* change, and deserves credit: the deleveraging commitment, the fuel-tank market-share march, and the free-cash-flow guidance. Management reaffirmed in July that full-year free cash flow will exceed the EUR 297 million delivered in 2025, having banked EUR 165 million in the first half.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

### 2a. The most important finding: the screening metrics handed to this committee are wrong, and wrong in the direction of making the stock look cheaper than it is

OPmobility is a French company that reports twice a year, not four times. The data vendor files each half-year report as a "quarter." Any process that builds a trailing-twelve-month figure by summing four filed periods therefore sums **two years**, not one. That is exactly what happened here:

| Metric as supplied | What it actually is | Corrected figure |
|---|---|---|
| "TTM diluted EPS 2.49" | The sum of four half-years: EUR 0.71 (H1-26) + 0.67 (H2-25) + 0.63 (H1-25) + 0.49 (H2-24) = 2.50 — two full years of earnings | **EUR 1.37** trailing twelve months to 2026-06-30 (net income EUR 197m) |
| "TTM FCF 890M" | The same doubling: EUR 262m + 183m + 271m + 174m = 890m — two years of cash flow | **EUR 445m** on the vendor's definition; **about EUR 310m** on the company's own definition |
| "P/FCF 4.0x" | Understated by the same mechanism | **About 4.1x** on the vendor's cash-flow definition, **about 5.8x** on the company's |

The consequence is direct. On the supplied earnings figure the shares look like they trade at roughly 5 times earnings. On the true trailing figure they trade at **9.2 times**. On the analyst consensus for this year (EUR 1.54 per share, from nine covering houses) they trade at **8.2 times**; on 2027 (EUR 1.74) at **7.3 times**; on 2028 (EUR 1.92) at **6.6 times**.

That is still inexpensive. It is not the extraordinary bargain the input file implies, and the "deep value" classification this name arrived with rests substantially on a doubled denominator. Everything downstream must be re-struck on the corrected numbers.

A second supplied metric is not wrong so much as meaningless: **"beat 0/6 qtrs (0%)."** A company that does not report quarterly earnings and has no quarterly consensus cannot miss a quarterly consensus. This is an artefact of the same semi-annual filing pattern, not evidence of a chronic disappointment habit. Read as written it would defame a management team whose actual delivery record (section 4) is good.

### 2b. Management's claims against the real numbers

| Claim (and where) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "This is the first time since 2019 that the group is able to exceed EUR 1 billion in EBITDA" (Feb-26, CFO Olivier Dabi) | Vendor data shows EUR 840m for 2025 on the consolidated basis; the EUR 1.001bn is struck on "economic revenue" of EUR 11.5bn, which includes the company's share of joint ventures. Trailing twelve months to June 2026 is EUR 913m consolidated. | **True but basis-shifted.** The claim is defensible on the company's chosen measure; a reader comparing it to consolidated peers will overstate the business by roughly 10%. |
| "The debt was reduced in '25 by EUR 167 million and amounted to EUR 1.4 billion" (Feb-26) | Balance sheet at 2025-12-31: net debt EUR 1.515bn including EUR 320m of capitalised leases; EUR 1.195bn excluding them. At 2026-06-30: EUR 1.433bn including EUR 308m of leases, EUR 1.125bn excluding. | **Verified, on the lease-excluding definition** — which is the definition the company quotes. The reduction is real and continued into 2026 (about EUR 82m in the first half against the "EUR 90 million" claimed). This is the cleanest claim in the file. |
| "Free cash flow of EUR 297 million, up an impressive 20% versus '24" (Feb-26); "we did EUR 165 million in S1, and we confirm our guidance to exceed last year's" (Jul-26) | The company's own cash-flow definition is stricter than the vendor's, which shows EUR 445m for the trailing twelve months by charging a smaller capital-spending figure. Cash and equivalents rose from EUR 671m (Dec-24) to EUR 815m (Jun-26) while debt fell — the cash is arriving. | **Corroborated in direction, and the more conservative company number is the one to use.** |
| "Solid operating margin of 4.8% of our revenues" (Jul-26) | The vendor's mapping gives first-half 2026 operating income of EUR 219m on EUR 5,202m — 4.2% — against EUR 260m on EUR 5,332m a year earlier. On the company's economic-revenue basis, 4.8% is above the 4.3% struck for full-year 2025 (EUR 490m on EUR 11.5bn). | **Unresolved, and flagged.** The two sources point in opposite directions. Given the vendor's demonstrated aggregation failure on this filer (section 2a) and its unstable expense mapping (research and development recorded at EUR 139m in the first half of 2025 and zero in the first half of 2026), I weight the company's figure — but this is a claim I could not independently close, and the committee should treat the operating-margin trend as unverified rather than confirmed. |
| Market-share gains: "market share in C-Power has increased from 21% to 23% in 2025... on track with the target we have of 30% by 2030" (Feb-26, Stéphanie Laval) | Not independently verifiable from the financials supplied. What *is* corroborating: fuel tanks led first-half 2026 growth, helped by "slower electrification that benefited this activity." | **Plausible and internally consistent**, but it is management's own market definition and cannot be audited here. |
| "We managed again to show a slight growth in a decrease in market... like-for-like sales, we had a slight increase of our sales of 0.2%" (Jul-26) | Reported first-half revenue fell 2.4% (EUR 5,202m against EUR 5,332m). The gap is currency: the company flagged EUR 300m of adverse foreign-exchange in 2025 alone, mostly a weaker dollar. | **Verified as stated.** The like-for-like claim is honest; the reported line is worse, and the reported line is what pays the debt. |

### 2c. The quality of the cash flow deserves a second look

First-half 2026 operating cash flow of EUR 423 million included a **positive EUR 97 million swing in working capital, driven by a EUR 335 million increase in accounts payable** — that is, paying suppliers more slowly. Receivables went the other way, consuming EUR 155 million. Analyst Ross MacDonald put the question squarely: "Do I understand that the working capital benefits in the first half, close to EUR 100 million should fully reverse for the full year metrics?"

The chief financial officer did not say no. He said: "We're still going to have a push on WCR with supplier payments initiative that we started. We're going to have lower factoring, but we will definitely improve the gross cash flow. So all in all, we'll see a transfer between WCR and gross cash flow to meet our objectives."

Two things are conceded there. First, the working-capital contribution is expected to unwind. Second — and this was volunteered, not extracted — **factoring will be lower in the second half**. Factoring is selling receivables to a bank early to pull cash forward; less of it is a genuine cash headwind. So the second-half free-cash-flow bridge depends on operating profit improving enough to offset both a working-capital reversal and less receivable financing, in a market management has just told us is running 2.3% below where they planned. The guidance may well be met. But it is being met by a narrower path than the first-half print suggests.

### 2d. Returns are the number that matters, and they are poor

Return on invested capital of 6.0% and return on equity of 8.1% (as supplied, and consistent with net income of EUR 197 million on EUR 2.19 billion of equity). A European industrial with EUR 2.2 billion of debt-funded capital and a 35% tax rate almost certainly has a cost of capital above 6%. **This business, on current returns, does not create value by growing.** That is the central tension: the operating story is one of resilience and share gain, and the return profile is one of a capital-intensive supplier running to stand still.

The tax rate compounds it. Asked directly in February whether 35% holds, the finance chief answered: "Yes. Tax rate should remain stable at 35% in '26. We aim to improve it a little bit, but it should stay within this ballpark." A third of pre-tax profit leaves permanently.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Declining — but declining honestly, which is a different and better thing than declining evasively.**

*February 2026* — offensive and specific. "I'm focused and determined to keep on executing our strategy." "We took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." "Impressive performance." The chief financial officer opened with "very strong results, very solid results." Guidance was concrete and referenced against prior commitments.

*July 2026* — the adjectives survive ("a solid set of figures") but every one now arrives escorted by a qualifier: "despite, as you know, a very complex environment we are surrounded with." The defensive vocabulary is dense — "resilience," "mitigate," "monitor," "adapt," "postponed," "competitiveness." The chief executive twice describes herself as watching rather than acting: "we are carefully monitoring," "we again have to monitor what could be the impact for the second half."

The clearest single tell is the shift in how the future is discussed. In February the horizon was a plan. In July it is a scenario set: "we keep on running different scenarios." On price recovery in the second half: "it's really hard to anticipate, and it will all depend on... how the situation evolves." On the Chinese market: "we are not expecting big changes."

Crucially, specificity did **not** collapse. The market forecast was restated with a number (−2.3%), the first-half cash figure was given (EUR 165m), the full-year guidance was reaffirmed against a named prior-year bar (EUR 297m), the seasonality question was answered directly ("we expect the numbers to be broadly in line in H2 versus H1"). Managements that are about to disappoint usually go vaguer, not more precise. This one went more precise while going more defensive. That combination reads as a team absorbing a worse market rather than one concealing an internal problem.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High — with one unproven item outstanding.**

The one full guidance cycle visible in this file closed cleanly. In February 2026 the finance chief stated: "all in all, our '25 metrics was achieved — were achieved in line with the guidance that we gave last year and that we reiterated throughout the year." Every checkable component of that is corroborated by the balance sheet and cash-flow statements: debt down EUR 167 million, free cash flow up about 20% to EUR 297 million, leverage from 1.7 to 1.4 times.

Into 2026, three commitments have been made and one has already been tested:
- **Free cash flow above EUR 297 million** — reaffirmed 2026-07-22 with EUR 165 million banked. Half-delivered; the second half depends on the bridge described in section 2c. **This is the unproven item.**
- **Continued deleveraging** — delivered again in the first half (about EUR 82 million reduction).
- **Tax rate near 35%** — held.

No sandbagging pattern is visible; if anything the opposite. Management reaffirmed a rising cash-flow target into a market that had deteriorated 2.3 percentage points below their own planning assumption, which is the harder choice. They also declined to over-claim on the second half's margin, answering the seasonality question with "broadly in line" rather than promising expansion.

The "beat 0 of 6 quarters" figure in the supplied metrics should be disregarded entirely, for the reason given in section 2a.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Four topics recur, and management's handling ranges from candid to conspicuously thin.

**1. The Hyundai Mobis transaction — answered least, matters most.** Raised on both calls and never quantified. In February: "I appreciate you can't give the numbers on the balance sheet impact from the M&A you announced recently with Hyundai Mobis." In July, Michael Foundoukidis pressed on whether it fits inside the deleveraging target, and got: "All of the figures that we're disclosing are without anything linked to this project. But as we said, we are taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy."

Read that carefully. It is an *objective*, not a commitment, and the numbers presented to the market explicitly exclude the deal. The single largest capital-allocation decision in front of this company sits entirely outside the disclosed financial picture, five months after announcement. That is the biggest information gap in the file.

**2. The Varroc precedent, which management raised itself.** The last sizeable acquisition was the 2022 lighting purchase, and the chief executive's own description of it is damning: Lighting "continued to suffer from the poor order book of — prior to the acquisition." That is a self-reported diligence failure — they bought a business whose forward order book was worse than they had underwritten. MacDonald asked the obvious follow-up: is Mobis different? The answer was assertion, not evidence: "the situation is totally — it's not comparable... Now what we are considering here is a very sizable business with 1 leading OEM. More than 90% of its sales engaged with that."

That sentence is meant to reassure and does the opposite. **A target deriving more than 90% of sales from a single carmaker is not the cure for a bad order book; it is a different concentration risk of comparable severity.** Management is trading order-book uncertainty for customer-concentration certainty and presenting the trade as de-risking.

**3. Working capital and the honesty of the cash flow.** MacDonald pushed on this in both calls and got a straighter answer than on Mobis — see section 2c. Analysts are clearly modelling a second-half reversal; management has not disputed it.

**4.
